result:
The lost-and-found at the train station had a drawer labeled **SOUNDS**.

Most of what came in was easy enough to identify. The click of a good pen. A dog shaking rain onto a kitchen floor. The little grunt a man makes when he sits down and discovers he’s older than he was yesterday.

Nobody ever came looking for those.

They came for the last thing their mother said, which they’d heard perfectly well at the time but hadn’t known to keep. They came for the noise their old apartment made at night, when the pipes knocked and the refrigerator quit humming and, for three or four seconds, the whole building seemed to be listening.

The clerk, whose name was Ida, would ask for a description.

“Was it a word or more of a breath?”

“Were you in the same room?”

“Did you turn around?”

That last question bothered people. Often they hadn’t.

One afternoon a little boy came in looking for the sound of his own laugh. He could still laugh, he explained, but lately, just as he was getting going, he’d hear himself and stop.

Ida opened the drawer. From somewhere beneath a loose bicycle bell came the sound of two grown women trying not to laugh at a funeral. One took a long, careful breath. The other made the mistake of whispering, “Don’t.”

The boy laughed. Then he put his hand over his mouth.

Ida waited.

From behind his hand came one more small, ridiculous snort. This time he took his hand away.
